title: Short Stuff: Joro Spiders
summary: Short Stuff episode on joro spiders (Trichonephila clavata, written here as Nephila clavata), an orb-weaving spider from East Asia now spreading across the southeastern and eastern US. hosts discuss how they arrived (likely in shipping containers and lumber), their spread from Georgia since about 2013 and into West Virginia and a satellite population near Baltimore, their size, large strong webs, and how to tell them apart from garden spiders. They cover Japanese and Korean names, female-only web spinning, male courtship behavior, the lack of clear ecological harm so far, and advice not to kill them. A CNN headline calling them giant venomous invaders is mocked. The episode ends with a brief bite anecdote and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and CNN headline
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, then a listener's sighting of a joro spider leads to a mock reaction to a CNN headline calling giant venomous joros an invasion.

segments.title: Origins, spread, and names
segments.summary: Joro spiders (Nephila clavata) came from East Asia likely via shipping containers and lumber, first spotted in Georgia around 2013 and now common in the Southeast. Japanese and Korean names are discussed.
topics: Japanese and Korean names for joro spiders

segments.title: Size, webs, and garden spider comparison
segments.summary: Joro webs can be several feet wide. Hosts compare joros with garden spiders, noting differences in color and size between females and males.

segments.title: Walking into webs and web strength
segments.summary: Hosts discuss walking into joro webs and how the webs are strong enough that birds can perch on them.

segments.title: Rapid spread and northern range
segments.summary: Joros are spreading fast, likely because predators have not yet found them, they have plentiful flying insects like stink bugs, and little competition. Their range has reached West Virginia and a population in Baltimore; University of Georgia research suggests they tolerate colder weather.

segments.title: Male courtship and cannibalism risk
segments.summary: Males live near females and approach them with tricks such as floating on silk. They risk being eaten by females, so they approach carefully. Males also glide on gossamer threads.

segments.title: Are joros harmful and should they be killed
segments.summary: Hosts say there is no clear evidence of major ecological harm and no apocalyptic impact so far. They advise against killing joros, which usually flee and whose venom is not dangerous to people.

segments.title: Bite anecdote and gardening gloves
segments.summary: Josh describes a relative who was bitten by a joro while deadheading roses, with a swollen hand. Chuck jokes about gardening gloves.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up and say short stuff is over; standard iHeartRadio credit follows.
